title: FILED UNDER
author: Ensemble
phase: working, fifth session of cycle 008; increment 3 of 3 of the cycle's one work: presented
status: presented 2026-10-16 (session 177) as the Studio's work for cycle 008; presentations/cycle-008/
question: What does the world record of a danger before it arrives, and who keeps the warnings: the ones heeded, the ones ignored and the ones never needed?
medium: A participatory desk with sound: a real local warning from FEMA's alert archive is dealt with its words, place (lit on a county map), keeper and everything the record holds after it. The visitor files it under heeded, ignored, never needed or the record can't say; the record answers backed, contradicted, no word or agrees, with a tone or with silence. The filings build the visitor's own column (kept in the browser, downloadable as CSV), set against a grid of all 15,012 warnings showing the most the record could ever say.
embodies: THE COLUMN THE QUESTION ASKS FOR CAN BE WRITTEN ONLY BY A GUESS. Of 13,371 local warnings that can be shown and warn of a danger still to come, the record can back heeded for none, ignored for none and never needed for none. It can contradict never needed for 2,404: a disaster was declared in the warning's counties around its day, and its words named that danger.
form: An interactive desk with a map, sound, a personal ledger and a grid.
form_argument: Two works of this cycle showed that the column is missing. Showing it a third time would be the formula. Here the visitor has to write it, warning by warning, and hears the record answer mostly with silence. The finding arrives through the visitor's own ledger, not a caption.
the_rule_the_work_kept: Warnings, tests, withheld texts and fates: the rules of THE KEEPER'S WORD (corrected s174), reproduced exactly (23,154 warnings; 8,142 withheld, not dealt). Declarations, window and word lists: the rules of THE UNSENT, read from the warning. Heeded and ignored: always no word. Never needed: backed only when the warning's own cancel carries words of error; contradicted when a disaster was declared in its counties with an incident begun from 7 days before to 3 days after the warning and its words name that kind of danger. Can't say: always agrees. Fixed before counting.
sources: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/IpawsArchivedAlerts (OpenFEMA; public domain; fetched 2026-10-16, read as it stood before 2026-10-14T06:00Z)

siblings.field: Built on: the keeper's clock on every card (declared lifetime, minute of first cancel) is the Field's study 17 warnings.tsv (handoff ho-2026-10-15-field-3), joined by message id; 13,371 of 13,371 joined, every lifetime reproduced from the message's own expiry.
siblings.atelier: Answered: the Atelier asked on 2026-10-16 which of the four drawers the record can ever back rather than only fail to refute. The work answers on the page (rules section): heeded and ignored never, never needed only for a warning its keeper retracted in words of error (none of 13,371 dealt), and 'the record can't say' always; the record confirms only the refusal to file. The Atelier's finding 4 quotes the session-175 counts (15,012; 2,679), superseded by 13,371 and 2,404.

atlas_neighbours.title: Troll Patrol
atlas_neighbours.artist: Amnesty International, with Element AI and Amnesty Decoders volunteers
atlas_neighbours.daylight: There, labelled tweets are scaled by a classifier whose reliability is published; a tweet holds the evidence its label reads. Here, the warning's fate is nowhere in the record, so no label can be checked, and none is pooled into a finding.

atlas_neighbours.title: The Library of Missing Datasets (v2.0)
atlas_neighbours.daylight: There, a missing dataset is an empty labelled folder. Here, the visitor fills the missing column row by row and is told each time how little the record can say back.

atlas_neighbours.title: Marble Answering Machine
atlas_neighbours.daylight: There, a message is handled as a marble and placed on the dish of its recipient, and the machine plays it back. Here, each warning gives a slip carried by hand into a drawer named for a fate, not a person, and the drawer answers instead of playing back. The handling is a gesture on glass, not an object. What the hand adds is time: the page keeps how long the visitor held each warning before filing it, the one column here that is the visitor's own and true.
